label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 12 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

rerun_command: python -m klaxon.evaluation run --model claude-opus-5-5 --cases pool-exhaustion --seeds 9 --steps 10 --tool-calls 8 --rate 3 --loop multi

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

alert.name: PaymentsErrorsHigh
alert.summary: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 87% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (4.52 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 7.4 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api's psycopg connection pool is exhausted. Every request that needs a DB connection waits about 5 s, then fails with PoolTimeout and returns 500. This explains both the 5xx rate and the p95 of 7.4 s on POST /payments. The most likely cause is the 21:42:25 payments-api deploy with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept: each successful refund appears to keep its connection instead of returning it. From about 21:41:35 to 21:43:30, refunds succeeded at about 0.13-0.44/s with no slow ones. Then refunds and payments began failing together at 21:43:35. Steady, fast refunds followed by a shared failure across routes fits connections being kept, not held during slow calls. The provider and Redis are fast. This mechanism is inferred from timing and the setting's name; no result shows pool usage.

evidence.shows: POST /payments 500s appear at 21:43:41 (1.1/s) and rise to 5.82/s at 21:44:11, while 201s fall from about 3/s to 0.
Every payments-api ERROR line for POST /payments in the sample has exception_type PoolTimeout: requests gave up waiting for a DB pool connection.
payments-api was redeployed at 21:42:25 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. Every other service dates from the 21:40:58 stack start.

arguments.query: sum by (http_route, http_request_method, http_response_status_code) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job=~".*payments-api.*"}[1m])) or sum by (http_route, http_request_method, http_response_status_code) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count[1m]))

evidence.shows: Refund 201s run at 0.13-0.44/s from 21:41:35, then drop to 0 by 21:44:05. Both /payments and /refunds start returning 500 at 21:43:35. The failure is shared across routes, as an empty pool would cause. The small 503s on /payments predate the 500s and are a separate effect.
Refund requests from 21:43:28 on take about 5.0-6.9 s, consistent with a 5 s pool wait timeout plus queueing.

A 5,008 ms refund trace holds only two Redis spans (under 1 ms each) and no DB or provider span. It ends with error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout, so it never got a connection and never reached the provider.
No successful refund took over 500 ms, so the pool is not draining because slow requests hold connections. This points to connections that are kept and never returned.

arguments.query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, http_request_method, server_address, http_response_status_code) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])))

evidence.shows: Provider call p95 stays at about 5-8 ms for both its 200s and its 500s, so fake-provider latency does not cause the waits.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 21:42:25 deploy, which should remove REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Recreating the container also drops every connection now held, so the pool starts empty. Afterwards, watch the POST /payments 5xx rate and p95 latency, and check that refund 201s keep going without the pool draining again. Then run the money check. Some payments or refunds may have failed after their provider call, and some 503s came from the breaker, so our books may be out of step with the provider's records. Still open: pool size and usage, and PostgreSQL connections and locks were never checked.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, and payments and refunds in flight at that moment fail. The rollback reverts all three settings from that deploy, not only REFUND_CONNECTION. PROVIDER_BREAKER goes back to its earlier value. CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT, which affects charged amounts, also goes back to whatever it was before, and no result shows that value. If REFUND_CONNECTION is not the real cause, the pool may drain again later. Money already booked wrong stays wrong.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy payments-api with the 21:42:25 settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept), as recorded in the deploy log. Restart it whenever the pool drains, until a fix that keeps the other two settings is ready.
